newsitem.title: USA: Allied purchase of Dauphin reflects trend.
newsitem.headline: Allied purchase of Dauphin reflects trend.

text.p: Allied Irish Banks Plc's planned purchase of Dauphin Deposit Corp reflects a larger trend of foreign banks that are casting an eye toward the consolidating U.S. market to diversify their businesses, analysts said Tuesday.

"The U.S. market is consolidating and foreign banks realize it will consolidate with or without them," said Marni Pont at Keefe Bruyette & Woods. "If there's acquisition activity they want to be involved in it."

Dublin-based Allied Irish said Tuesday its U.S. unit, First Maryland Bancorp, would acquire Dauphin, based in Harrisburg, Pa., for $1.36 billion, a price-to-earnings multiple of 19.1 times 1996 earnings.
Officials at First Maryland and Dauphin were unavailable for comment.
Shares of Dauphin rose 5-5/8 to close at 41-1/8 on Nasdaq. Dauphin is the fourth largest commercial bank in Pennsylvania with total assets of $6 billion.

Analysts gave a thumbs-up to the purchase price because shareholders can elect to exchange each share they hold for $43 in cash. They said the acquisition will give Allied Irish a strong market presence in central Pennsylvania.
"It's a very high purchase price and it's going to be good for shareholders," said Jim Schutz at ABN AMRO Chicago Corp.
"We were delighted that Dauphin was sold."
Schutz said the two banks combined will have a 37 percent market share in York County, Pa.
"Dauphin has been considered a premier acquisition (target) in Pennsylvania. They have a terrific market presence."
Allied Irish expects to close the acquisition in the third quarter of 1997.
Analysts said the two combined banks also will be able to cut costs by consolidating branches. Dauphin operates 98 branches in south central Pennsylvania.
"This will represent about $48 million in cost savings over the next two years," Schutz said.
Analysts said Dauphin has strong businesses in both consumer and commercial financial services, something that will be a plus for Allied Irish.
"Their consumer and commercial business lines are pretty robust," said Kevin Timmons at First Albany Corp. "They know their markets well."
Timmons said foreign banks have become more active in the past two years in the U.S. market and the acquisition will give Allied Irish a solid presence in the mid-Atlantic region.
"Foreign banks are trying to diversify outside of their own markets and the U.S. is good business territory," he said.
"An institution of Dauphin's size, it's big enough (for Allied Irish) to make an impact (in the U.S. market.")
